paragraphs: We have already reported that Abū ʿĪsā laid claim to prophethood, and that his miracle, with his adherents, was that he was an illiterate who could neither write nor read, yet brought forth books and scrolls — and that this can be only by prophethood. As for his doctrines and statements: he forbade the divorce explicitly permitted [in Scripture] — as the Sadducees and Christians forbade it — and made obligatory seven prayers each day, going in this to the saying of David [Ps 119:164]: "שֶׁבַע בַּיּוֹם הִלַּלְתִּיךָ עַל מִשְׁפְּטֵי צִדְקֶךָ." He forbade meat and [wine-]drinking — not from Scripture, but by claiming that God commanded him so by prophecy. He greatly strengthened and magnified the matter of the Rabbanites, until he placed them in something resembling the rank of the prophets, and claimed that God told him to pray with the Eighteen [Benedictions] and with the recital of the Shemaʿ, as the Rabbanites say. He did this only to win over, by means of it, the hearts of the commonalty and the majority. For this reason the Rabbanites and the majority do not [much] reckon with the ʿĪsawiyya, and do not regard them with the eye with which they regard the ʿAnanites and the Karaites.
§2 — The question to Jacob ben Ephraim

I once asked "Jacob ben Ephraim al-Shāmī," saying to him: "Why did you draw the ʿĪsawiyya near and intermarry with them — they being upon what you know, ascribing prophethood to one not fit for it?" He said: "Because they did not dissent from us in the festivals." So this indicates that the appearance of unbelief, with people, is easier [to bear] than the appearance of dissension in a festival that they have innovated. Abū ʿĪsā acknowledged the prophethood of "Jesus son of Mary" and the prophethood of the prophet of the Muslims, claiming that each of them was sent to his own people and commanded the reading of the Gospel and the Qurʾān and the knowledge of their interpretations; and he claimed that the Muslims and the Christians — each nation of them was bound by what is in their hands, as Judaism was bound by what is in theirs. What brought him to acknowledge the prophethood of these two persons was a safeguard for his case and a shield for his words and for what he claimed of prophecy; for had he given them the lie and not acknowledged them, men would have been quicker to deny him. So his affirming of the two was in the hope that in it would be the completion of his case; but what he hoped of this came to nothing, and his hope was cut off. We shall make clear the corruption of his claim and the falsity of his statement later.
: Seven prayers a day — a starting point for the ʿĪsawiyya; compare the supererogatory prayers in Karaism.
: The Eighteen Benedictions — the rabbinic ʿAmidah; Abū ʿĪsā adopted it, per Q, to align himself with the rabbinic majority.

: A notable social observation: the Rabbanites tolerated the ʿĪsawiyya (who claimed prophethood and messiahship) because they did not dissent on the festival calendar — but rejected the Karaites, who offered only rational inquiry yet dissented on the calendar.
: Jacob ben Ephraim al-Shāmī, a Syrian Rabbanite contemporary of Q; not well known in the scholarship.
: The story of Abū ʿĪsā's frustrated hopes — that he sought authority through Muḥammad's and Jesus' recognition, and failed. Cf. Erder, "The Doctrine of Abū ʿĪsā," JSAI 20 (1996).
